lessons.title: Pattern Making and Cutting
lessons.body:
Pattern making starts with a paper template. Use brown paper or manila card. For a simple tote bag, measure 35 cm wide by 40 cm tall for the body. Add 1 cm seam allowance on all sides. Cut two body pieces. For the handles, cut two strips 60 cm long and 4 cm wide. Always make a test pattern from cheap fabric or cardboard before cutting leather. Leather is expensive; a mistake wastes money.

Gather your tools: a sharp craft knife or round knife, cutting mat, metal ruler, pencil, and pattern weights. Place your pattern on the leather's flesh side (the back). Trace around it with a pencil or silver pen. Avoid ballpoint pens; they smudge. For dark leather, use a white chalk pencil. Mark all stitch lines and hardware holes. Remember: leather stretches, so cut slightly larger than needed if unsure.

Cutting technique: use a sharp blade. Dull blades tear the leather and cause jagged edges. Make long, smooth cuts. For curves, use a round knife or a head knife. Always cut on a cutting mat or thick cardboard to protect your table. If you have a strap cutter, use it for belts and handles. For thin leather (1-2 mm), you can use scissors, but for thick leather (3-4 mm), a knife is better.

In Africa, many artisans use locally available tools: a sharpened machete for rough cutting, or a tailors' scissors. But invest in a good round knife when you can. It costs about 20-30 USD and lasts years. Also, consider the leather's grain. Cut patterns so the stretch direction goes across the bag, not along it, to avoid sagging. For small items like wallets, you can nest patterns to save leather. Always cut on a clean surface. After cutting, label each piece with a pencil (e.g., 'front', 'back', 'handle'). This prevents confusion during stitching.

Practice on scrap leather first. Cut straight lines, curves, and corners. Aim for smooth edges. A good cut saves time in edge finishing. Remember: measure twice, cut once. In production, one wrong cut can ruin a whole hide. So take your time.

lessons.title: Stitching and Assembly
lessons.body:
Stitching leather is different from sewing fabric. You need a saddle stitch, which is strong and won't unravel if one thread breaks. Tools: two harness needles (size 0 or 1), waxed linen thread (0.8 mm thick), stitching awl, stitching pony (to hold work), and a diamond chisel or overstitch wheel to mark holes. For a beginner, a stitching chisel with 4 prongs (2 mm spacing) is good. You will also need a mallet and a cutting mat.

First, mark your stitch line. Use a wing divider or a stitch groover to make a groove 3-4 mm from the edge. Then, use the chisel to punch holes. Place the chisel on the line, hit with mallet, and move along. Keep spacing even. For curves, use a 2-prong chisel. Alternatively, use an awl to make holes as you stitch. For a saddle stitch, cut thread about 4 times the length of the seam. Thread a needle on each end. Push one needle through the first hole, pull to center. Then push the other needle through the same hole from the opposite side. Pull both tight. Continue: one needle through next hole, then the other from the other side. Always pull in the same direction to avoid tangles.

Assembly order matters. For a bag, stitch the gusset (side piece) to the front and back panels. Then attach the handle. Use contact cement (like Barge or local rubber cement) to glue edges before stitching. This holds pieces in place. Apply glue thinly, wait 10-15 minutes until tacky, then press together. Hammer the seam lightly to set. Then stitch. For wallets, stitch the card slots first, then assemble. Use a stitching pony to hold the work; it frees both hands.

In Africa, many artisans use a sewing machine for leather, but only for thin leather (1-2 mm). For thick leather, hand stitching is better. A walking foot machine is ideal. If using a machine, use a leather needle (size 90/14 or 100/16) and heavy-duty thread (like bonded nylon). Test on scrap. For hand stitching, practice on scrap until your stitches are even. A good saddle stitch is tight and uniform. It takes time: about 1 hour for a small bag. But it's a skill worth mastering. Remember: the thread should be waxed to reduce friction and increase durability. You can wax your own thread with beeswax.

lessons.title: Edge Finishing and Burnishing
lessons.body:
Edge finishing makes your product look professional. Raw edges are ugly and prone to fraying. Start by trimming the edge flush with a sharp knife or edge beveler. An edge beveler (size 1 or 2) removes the sharp corner, creating a rounded edge. Then sand the edge with fine sandpaper (400 grit), then 600, then 800. Sand in one direction. Wipe away dust with a damp cloth.

Next, apply edge paint or burnish. For burnishing, you need a wooden slicker or a canvas cloth. Dampen the edge with water or gum tragacanth (a natural gum). Rub vigorously with the slicker or canvas until the edge becomes smooth and shiny. This works well on vegetable-tanned leather. For chrome-tanned leather, burnishing doesn't work well; use edge paint instead. Apply edge paint in thin layers. Let dry 10 minutes between coats. Use 2-3 coats. Then polish with a cloth. For a high-end look, use beeswax and a heated edge iron.

In Africa, you can make your own edge slicker from hard wood (like mahogany) by carving a groove. Or use a piece of denim. Gum tragacanth is available in some craft shops, but you can substitute with a little soapy water. For edge paint, local shoe repair shops often sell it. Alternatively, use a mixture of beeswax and paraffin wax. Melt together, apply to edge, and rub with a cloth. This gives a rustic finish.

Edge finishing takes time: about 10-15 minutes per edge. But it's what separates amateur from professional. For belts, burnish both sides. For bags, focus on visible edges. Always test on scrap first. If the edge looks fuzzy, sand more. If it's uneven, trim again. A good edge is smooth, rounded, and slightly darker than the leather. It should feel like a single piece, not layers. Remember: sharp tools are essential. A dull edge beveler will tear the leather. Sharpen on a fine whetstone. Also, keep your work clean. Dust and glue residue ruin the finish. So wipe edges before burnishing. With practice, you can finish edges quickly and consistently.

lessons.title: Hardware and Lining
lessons.body:
Hardware includes buckles, rivets, snaps, D-rings, and zippers. Choose solid brass or nickel-plated hardware for durability. Avoid cheap pot metal; it breaks. For bags, use 1-inch D-rings for straps. For belts, use a 1.5-inch buckle. For wallets, use 0.5-inch snaps. Install rivets with a rivet setter and anvil. Place the rivet through holes, then hammer the setter to flare the post. For snaps, use a snap setter. Practice on scrap first.

Lining adds structure and a finished look. Common lining materials: pigskin, suede, or fabric like canvas. For a bag, cut lining the same size as the leather pieces, minus seam allowance. Glue lining to the flesh side with contact cement. Then stitch around edges. For wallets, line card slots with thin leather. For belts, no lining needed. When lining, make sure the lining is slightly smaller to avoid bunching. Use a walking foot machine or hand stitch. If hand stitching, glue first and stitch through both layers.

In Africa, you can source hardware from local markets or online. In Nairobi, check Kamukunji market; in Lagos, Balogun market. For lining, use local goat leather or cotton fabric. For zippers, use YKK or local brands. Install zippers with a zipper foot on a sewing machine. Or hand stitch with a backstitch. For a simple tote, you can skip lining and just burnish the inside. But lining hides the rough flesh side and adds value. For a professional look, line at least the main compartment.

When attaching hardware, reinforce the leather. For D-rings, fold a strap over the ring and rivet it. Or stitch a patch. For snaps, add a small piece of leather behind the snap to prevent tearing. For buckles, use a chape (a leather loop) and stitch. Always test hardware strength by pulling. A bag handle should hold at least 10 kg. Use two rivets per handle for safety. For zippers, ensure the slider moves smoothly. If it sticks, rub with wax. Remember: hardware placement affects balance. For a shoulder bag, place D-rings at the sides, about 5 cm from the top. For a belt, the buckle goes at one end, holes at the other. Measure twice before punching holes. A good hardware job makes your product last for years.

lessons.title: Quality Checks in Production
lessons.body:
Quality checks prevent returns and build reputation. Check each product at every stage. After cutting, check for flaws: scars, holes, or uneven thickness. Reject defective pieces. After stitching, inspect seams: they should be straight, tight, and even. No skipped stitches or loose threads. Run your finger along the seam; it should feel smooth. Check edges: they should be burnished or painted evenly. No glue stains or scratches. For hardware, test snaps and zippers. They should open and close smoothly. Pull on D-rings and rivets; they must not move. For lined items, ensure lining is not wrinkled or loose.

Use a checklist. For a bag: check dimensions (e.g., 35x40 cm), handle length (60 cm), stitch count (8-10 stitches per inch), and hardware function. For a wallet: check card slots (fit a card snugly), snap alignment, and edge finish. For a belt: check length (e.g., 100 cm), hole spacing (2.5 cm), and buckle attachment. Measure with a tape. Weigh the product if needed. A standard tote should weigh about 500 g. If too heavy, hardware is too big. If too light, leather is too thin.

In Africa, quality control is often informal. But for export or high-end markets, you need consistency. Set up a simple inspection station with good lighting. Use a magnifying lamp to check stitches. Train one person as quality inspector. They should sign off on each item. Keep records: date, product, inspector, defects found. This helps trace problems. For example, if a batch of belts has loose rivets, you know which rivet setter was used. Also, do a final check after packaging. Open one item per batch to ensure it meets standards. If you find a defect, fix it or discard. Never sell a defective product; it damages your brand.

Common defects: uneven stitching (caused by dull needle or inconsistent tension), burned edges (from too much friction), and misaligned hardware (from wrong measurement). To avoid, maintain tools, measure carefully, and practice. For hand stitching, use a stitching pony to keep work steady. For machine stitching, adjust tension on scrap first. For edges, don't over-burnish; it can crack. For hardware, use the right size setter. A quality product feels solid and looks clean. It should have no loose threads, no glue marks, and no sharp edges. Remember: your name is on it. So check every item as if you were the customer.

lessons.title: Packaging and Storage
lessons.body:
Packaging protects your product and sells it. Use a dust bag made of cotton or flannel. For a bag, a drawstring dust bag costs about 1-2 USD. You can sew your own from local fabric. For wallets, use a small box or a paper sleeve. Add a care card: instructions to clean with leather conditioner and avoid water. For belts, roll them and tie with a ribbon. For high-end products, use a rigid box with tissue paper. In Africa, you can source boxes from local printers. Print your logo with a rubber stamp or sticker. Keep packaging simple but professional.

Storage is critical. Leather is sensitive to moisture, heat, and sunlight. Store in a cool, dry place. Ideal temperature: 20-25Â°C. Humidity: 50-60%. Avoid direct sunlight; it fades color. Use shelves, not floor. Keep products in dust bags. For long-term storage, stuff bags with tissue paper to hold shape. For belts, hang them or roll loosely. Never store leather in plastic bags; it traps moisture and causes mold. If mold appears, wipe with a vinegar-water solution (1:1) and dry away from heat. For hardware, wrap in tissue to prevent scratches. If stacking, place heavier items at bottom.

In Africa, many artisans work in humid climates. Use silica gel packets in storage bins. You can buy them in bulk online. Also, use a dehumidifier if possible. For small workshops, a simple cabinet with a door works. Keep away from kitchens and bathrooms. If you ship products, use padded envelopes or boxes. For international shipping, declare as 'handmade leather goods' and include a commercial invoice. Use a courier like DHL or local post. Insure high-value shipments. For local markets, use a reusable tote bag with your logo. This doubles as advertising.

Labeling: include your brand, material (e.g., 'genuine cowhide'), and country of origin. For export, follow labeling laws. For example, in the EU, you must state if leather is 'genuine' or 'bonded'. Also, include a batch number for traceability. For pricing, factor in packaging cost: about 5-10% of product price. Good packaging increases perceived value. A product in a nice box can sell for 20% more. So invest in quality packaging. But don't overdo it; keep it eco-friendly. Use recycled paper and natural fabrics. Finally, store finished goods away from tools and chemicals. Keep a clean, organized space. This prevents damage and makes packing easy.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Leather Product Manufacturing

This practical reference module consolidates the core operational knowledge required to manufacture finished leather goods â from pattern making through to packaging and storage. It is written for African leather entrepreneurs, workshop managers, and artisan-entrepreneurs who want to move beyond raw hide trading into higher-value finished products: bags, belts, sandals, wallets, and accessories. The focus throughout is on practical decisions that affect cost, quality, and market access.

Africa produces a significant share of the world's raw hides and skins, yet captures only a small fraction of the finished leather goods market. The African Leather and Leather Products Industry (ALLPI) estimates that less than 10% of leather produced on the continent is processed into finished goods locally. This module is designed to help you capture more of that value chain in your own workshop.

Pattern Making and Cutting

Pattern making is the foundation of consistent, repeatable production. A pattern is a template â usually made from cardboard, MDF, or heavy acetate â that defines the shape of each component of a product. Without accurate patterns, every unit you produce will vary, and variance kills profitability in a workshop that relies on repeat orders.

Key principles:

  • Start from a finished sample. Deconstruct an existing product you admire (or your own prototype) and trace each panel onto pattern board. Add seam allowance â typically 6â10 mm for hand-stitched goods, 4â6 mm for machine-stitched.
  • Mark grain direction. Leather stretches differently along and across the backbone. Patterns must indicate grain direction so panels are cut consistently.
  • Nest patterns efficiently. Hide is expensive. A poorly nested cutting layout can waste 20â30% of a hide. Use chalk or a marker to lay out patterns before cutting.
  • Cut on a cutting mat or board, never directly on concrete. Use a sharp head knife or rotary cutter. Dull tools tear grain and create ragged edges that are expensive to finish.

Stitching and Assembly

Stitching transforms flat panels into a three-dimensional product. In African workshops, both hand-stitching (saddle stitch) and machine stitching (flat-bed or cylinder-arm) are common. The choice depends on product type, volume, and available capital.

Hand stitching remains the gold standard for luxury and heritage goods. It requires two needles, waxed thread (usually linen or polyester), and a stitching pony or clamp. The saddle stitch is stronger than a machine lock-stitch because if one thread breaks, the other holds. For belts, wallets, and small accessories, hand stitching commands a premium price in export markets.

Machine stitching is faster and more consistent for high-volume production. A walking-foot machine (compound feed) is essential for leather because it prevents the layers from shifting. Common stitch types include lock-stitch (Class 301) and chain-stitch (Class 401). For bags and upholstery, a cylinder-arm machine allows you to stitch around curves and into corners.

Practical assembly sequence:

  1. Skive (thin) edges where panels overlap to reduce bulk.
  2. Glue panels temporarily with contact adhesive or rubber cement.
  3. Punch stitch holes with a pricking iron or use a stitching chisel.
  4. Stitch from the center outward to prevent distortion.
  5. Backstitch at the beginning and end for security.

Edge Finishing and Burnishing

Edge finishing is what separates amateur work from professional work. Raw cut edges are porous, absorb dirt, and look unfinished. Proper edge finishing seals the leather, protects it from moisture, and gives a polished, market-ready appearance.

Steps for a professional edge:

  1. Trim and sand. Use a sharp edge beveler to create a rounded profile, then sand with 400â800 grit paper.
  2. Apply edge paint or gum. For painted edges, apply two to three thin coats of edge paint (water-based or solvent-based), drying between coats. For natural edges, apply gum tragacanth or a burnishing gum.
  3. Burnish. Rub vigorously with a wooden slicker, canvas cloth, or edge burnisher. Friction generates heat, which seals the fibers.
  4. Wax and polish. Apply beeswax or paraffin and buff with a cloth for a glossy finish.

In African markets, edge finishing is often the single biggest differentiator between a product that sells for $15 and one that sells for $50. Invest in good edge tools and practice until the finish is uniform.

Hardware and Lining

Hardware â buckles, rivets, snaps, D-rings, zippers, and magnetic closures â must be selected for both aesthetics and function. In humid African climates, choose solid brass or stainless steel over cheap plated alloys that corrode quickly. A tarnished buckle on a new bag destroys customer trust.

Lining protects the interior of bags and improves perceived quality. Common lining materials include pigskin, goat suede, cotton canvas, and synthetic fabrics. For tropical climates, natural breathable linings are preferred over plastic-based ones that trap moisture and cause mold.

Table 1: Common Leather Hardware â Selection Guide for African Climates
Hardware Type Recommended Material Typical Use Durability in Humidity
BucklesSolid brass, stainless steelBelts, bag strapsExcellent
RivetsCopper, brassReinforcement pointsVery good
Snaps / MagneticNickel-plated brassClosures, flapsGood (plating may wear)
ZippersBrass or YKK metalPockets, main closuresVery good
D-ringsSolid brass, stainlessStrap attachmentsExcellent

Source: Compiled from ITC, Leather Goods: International Trade and Market Trends (Geneva: International Trade Centre, 2019), Annex 3; and ALLPI, Leather Value Addition Handbook (Addis Ababa: African Leather and Leather Products Industry, 2021), pp. 44â46.

Quality Checks in Production

Quality control must be built into every stage, not inspected at the end. A defect discovered after assembly wastes labor, materials, and time. Implement in-process checks at four key points: after cutting, after stitching, after edge finishing, and before packaging.

Table 2: In-Process Quality Checkpoints for Leather Goods Manufacturing
Stage Check Common Defect Corrective Action
CuttingPattern accuracy, grain directionMisaligned panelsRe-trace pattern, check grain arrow
StitchingStitch length, tension, alignmentLoose or skipped stitchesAdjust tension, replace needle
Edge FinishingUniformity, smoothness, colorRough or uneven edgesRe-sand, re-apply edge paint
HardwareSecurity, function, finishLoose rivets, scratched bucklesRe-set rivets, replace hardware
FinalOverall appearance, dimensionsDimension drift, stainsReject or rework before packing

Source: Adapted from UNIDO, Leather Products Manufacturing: A Technical Guide for Small and Medium Enterprises (Vienna: UNIDO, 2010), Table 7.1, p. 112; and ISO 9001:2015 quality management principles as applied to artisan production.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Chemical and Tool Hazards

Leather work involves sharp tools (head knives, awls, edge bevelers), contact adhesives with toxic solvents, and edge paints that may contain harmful compounds. Always wear cut-resistant gloves when cutting, work in a well-ventilated area when using adhesives or solvent-based finishes, and store chemicals away from food and children. In many African workshops, ventilation is poor â install a fan or work outdoors when applying solvent-based products. Never burn leather scraps indoors; chromium-tanned leather releases toxic fumes when burned.

Packaging and Storage

Packaging protects your product, communicates your brand, and influences the buyer's perception of value. For local markets, simple kraft paper or reusable cloth bags with a branded stamp work well. For export or premium retail, invest in dust bags, tissue paper, and rigid boxes.

Storage best practices:

  • Store finished goods in a cool, dry place â ideally 15â25Â°C with relative humidity below 60%.
  • Use silica gel packets in storage bins to absorb moisture.
  • Keep leather away from direct sunlight, which fades dyes and dries the material.
  • Do not stack heavy items on top of finished bags; use shelves or hanging racks.
  • Rotate stock (first in, first out) to prevent old inventory from degrading.

In humid coastal cities like Mombasa, Lagos, or Dar es Salaam, mold is a serious risk. Invest in a dehumidifier or use well-sealed plastic bins with desiccant packs. A moldy product cannot be sold at full price â prevention is far cheaper than remediation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Patterns are traced on rigid board with grain direction marked and seam allowance added.
  2. Cutting layout nests patterns efficiently; hide waste is under 20%.
  3. Stitch length is consistent (typically 6â8 stitches per inch for hand stitching).
  4. Edges are sanded, painted or gummed, burnished, and waxed.
  5. Hardware is solid brass or stainless steel â no cheap plated alloys in humid climates.
  6. Lining is breathable and appropriate for tropical conditions.
  7. In-process quality checks are done after cutting, stitching, edge finishing, and before packing.
  8. Finished goods are stored below 60% humidity with silica gel and away from sunlight.

Further Reading

  • UNIDO â Leather Products Manufacturing: A Technical Guide for SMEs (free PDF, comprehensive technical reference)
  • African Leather and Leather Products Industry (ALLPI) â continental body supporting leather value addition; training materials and country reports
  • International Trade Centre (ITC) â market analysis, export guides, and trade data for leather goods
  • FAO â Leather and Leather Products â technical guidance on hides, skins, and processing
  • Leather Working Group (LWG) â environmental and quality standards for leather manufacturing

Business takeaway: The African leather goods market is growing, driven by rising middle-class demand, fashion exports, and import substitution. Your competitive advantage lies in craftsmanship, consistency, and local material knowledge. Master the practical skills in this module, document your quality standards, and price for the value you deliver â not for the cheapest possible unit. A well-finished leather bag made in Nairobi or Addis Ababa can compete with anything made in Milan or Guangzhou when the craft is right.

quiz.q: What is the first step in pattern making for a leather bag?
quiz.explanation: A paper template allows you to test the design before cutting expensive leather.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a ballpoint pen to trace patterns on leather?
options: B) It smudges and ruins the leather
C) It is not available in Africa
quiz.explanation: Ballpoint ink smudges easily and can stain the leather permanently.

quiz.q: What type of knife is recommended for cutting curves in leather?
quiz.explanation: A round knife allows smooth curved cuts, while utility knives are for straight lines.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding seam allowance to a pattern?
options: A) To make the product larger
quiz.explanation: Seam allowance provides extra material that is consumed during stitching.

quiz.q: Which stitch is strongest for leather assembly?
quiz.explanation: The saddle stitch is a two-needle hand stitch that will not unravel if one thread breaks.

quiz.q: What tool holds leather work steady while hand stitching?
quiz.explanation: A stitching pony clamps the work, freeing both hands for stitching.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thread length for a saddle stitch?
quiz.explanation: Four times the seam length provides enough thread to stitch without running out.

quiz.q: Why is contact cement used before stitching?
options: A) To make the leather waterproof
B) To hold pieces in place
quiz.explanation: Contact cement temporarily bonds pieces so they don't shift during stitching.

quiz.q: Which machine is best for sewing thick leather?
quiz.explanation: A walking foot machine moves the leather evenly, preventing skipped stitches.

quiz.q: What is the first step in edge finishing?
quiz.explanation: Trimming the edge flush creates a clean base for further finishing.

quiz.q: Which leather type responds best to burnishing?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable-tanned leather has natural fibers that burnish to a smooth shine.

quiz.q: What can be used as a substitute for gum tragacanth in burnishing?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water provides lubrication for burnishing when gum tragacanth is unavailable.

quiz.q: How many coats of edge paint are typically needed?
quiz.explanation: Two to three thin coats give a smooth, durable edge finish.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an edge beveler?
options: B) To round the sharp edge
quiz.explanation: An edge beveler removes the sharp corner, creating a rounded edge that burnishes better.

quiz.q: Which hardware material is most durable?
quiz.explanation: Solid brass resists corrosion and holds up to heavy use.

quiz.q: What tool is used to set rivets?
quiz.explanation: A rivet setter flares the rivet post to secure it.

quiz.q: Why should you reinforce leather where hardware is attached?
options: A) To make it look pretty
quiz.explanation: Reinforcement distributes stress and prevents the leather from tearing under load.

quiz.q: What is a common lining material for leather bags?
quiz.explanation: Pigskin is thin, durable, and commonly used as a lining in leather goods.

quiz.q: How much weight should a well-made bag handle hold?
quiz.explanation: A handle should hold at least 10 kg to be considered strong and safe.

quiz.q: Where should D-rings be placed on a shoulder bag?
options: B) At the sides, 5 cm from top
quiz.explanation: Placing D-rings at the sides near the top balances the bag when carried.

quiz.q: What is the first quality check after cutting leather?
options: A) Check for scars and holes
quiz.explanation: Defective leather pieces should be rejected before assembly to save time.

quiz.q: How many stitches per inch are typical for quality leather work?
quiz.explanation: 8-10 stitches per inch is a standard density for strong, attractive seams.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a loose rivet during quality check?
quiz.explanation: Loose hardware is a defect that must be fixed to ensure product safety.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in quality control?
quiz.explanation: Records help identify which batch or worker caused a defect for corrective action.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of uneven stitching?
quiz.explanation: A dull needle can skip stitches and create uneven spacing.

quiz.q: What should you use to stuff a bag for storage?
quiz.explanation: Tissue paper holds the shape without adding weight or moisture.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity for storing leather?
quiz.explanation: 50-60% humidity prevents drying and cracking while inhibiting mold growth.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid storing leather in plastic bags?
options: B) It traps moisture and causes mold
quiz.explanation: Plastic bags trap moisture, creating a breeding ground for mold.

quiz.q: What is a good way to label a leather product for export?
quiz.explanation: Export regulations often require clear labeling of material and country of origin.

quiz.q: How much of the product price should packaging cost?
quiz.explanation: Spending 5-10% on packaging adds perceived value without cutting too much into profit.
